tagline: Chapel country, where the men and the women used separate doors.
intro: The mapped road comes down through Jackson and over the hills to Kanauga, on the Ohio across from Point Pleasant, and the byway's chapels lie along it and on side roads toward Oak Hill and Centerville. This was Welsh country. The first of them, the 1818 Welsh, stopped at Gallipolis to mend a flatboat bound for Paddy's Run near Cincinnati and never left, and more than 3,000 followed in the 1830s and 1840s.

Many of their chapels had two front doors, because men and women sat on opposite sides, and a tea house, the ty capel, for feeding the minister. They also fired charcoal iron furnaces, until richer ores in Michigan and Minnesota brought Ohio's iron industry to an end.

moments.title: Jackson
moments.text: John Wesley Powell spent his formative years in Jackson, and in 1938 the square got a memorial to him built of stones given by tribes of the Improved Order of Red Men.

moments.title: Centerville Hill Cemetery
moments.text: Many of the first Welsh settlers lie on this hilltop a mile outside Centerville, which began when the widow Thomas gave the land and had her husband moved up from the village cemetery.

moments.title: Rio Grande
moments.text: Pronounced Rye-O Grand, the village flies a flag identical to the Flag of Wales, and the first Bob Evans restaurant began here as a single truck stop diner.
